fatal_errors: The proposed post-solidification anneal cannot improve glass-forming ability as conventionally defined, because it is applied only after an amorphous ribbon has already formed; it could at most alter amorphous-state stability.
The intervention does not reconstruct the demonstrated strategy of changing Fe/Co/Mn/P composition and using rapid melt spinning to suppress segregation and phosphide formation.
The prescription of 0.8Tg is inapplicable to the target alloy because no glass transition was detected, so Tg and therefore the proposed annealing temperature cannot be established.

None of the cited evidence demonstrates that sub-Tg annealing raises crystallization onset or promotes crystallization-resistant short-range order in these phosphorus-containing compositionally complex alloys.
explanation: The response addresses a phosphorus-containing melt-spun glass and proposes a testable control comparison, but it misses the target intervention, baseline, processing conditions, and phase-selection mechanism. The target improvement arose from adjusting Fe/Co/Mn ratios, reducing P from 20 to 15 at.%, and rapidly quenching at 40 m/s, which shifted solidification toward a dominant eutectic pathway and suppressed elemental partitioning and phosphide nucleation. By contrast, the proposed anneal assumes a measurable Tg that the target material did not exhibit and conflates post-formation structural relaxation with improved glass formation. Its evidence establishes only that rapid quenching can produce an amorphous ribbon and that heating can crystallize amorphous material; it does not support the claimed annealing effect. DSC/XRD/TEM comparisons could assess thermal stability, but the experiment does not test glass-forming ability unless independently cast samples are evaluated at reduced cooling rates or increased thickness after the intervention, which is impossible for a treatment applied after casting.
